English: Stone Bath
A basic ritual bathing site, constructed with crudely stacked stones and filled from nearby streams or wells. Used by the faithful for ritual purification even in the harshest conditions.
Water Storage
Improved ritual bath with lined pits and clay jars for storing water, ensuring the community has a reliable supply for purification even during drought or migration.
Ritual Pool
A larger, partially dug-out ritual pool lined with stones and basic wooden planks, enabling more extensive and communal purification ceremonies on the move.
Heated Chamber
A covered and semi-permanent bath structure, featuring primitive heating (stone hearths or clay ovens) for comfort and year-round ritual immersion, even in cold climates.
Changing Room
A dedicated tent or wooden enclosure for privacy, allowing for dignified preparation before and after ritual immersion, reinforcing communal cohesion.
Private Bath Pavilion
A more elaborate structure with partitions for private immersion, reserved for elders and prominent clan members, fostering respect for tradition and leadership.
Community Bathhouse
A semi-permanent communal bathhouse with stone or mud-brick walls, proper drainage, and a water channel, serving as a center for ritual purity and clan gatherings.
Family Bath Hall
A spacious, well-constructed hall with distinct areas for families and gender-segregated ritual immersion, reflecting developed nomadic piety and unity.
Sanctified Bath Room
A highly sanctified and adorned bath chamber, blessed by religious authorities, drawing pilgrims and conferring great honor and unity upon the clan.
Mikveh

The pinnacle of ritual bathing—a masterfully constructed, halachically pure mikveh that serves as both a spiritual and social heart for the nomadic Jewish clan, radiating sanctity and unity across the steppe.
